title: St. Louis Blues
origin: American blues / early jazz -- the first great published blues, a multi-strain song whose G-minor habanera middle section is Handy's famous 'Spanish tinge'

pd.detail: First published 1914 by Pace & Handy Music Co., Memphis.
pd.sourceEdition: Handy, W. C., 'Saint Louis Blues', Pace & Handy Music Co., 1914 piano/vocal sheet; changes cross-checked against common-practice fake-book charts of the same strains.
pd.notes: Chart only: changes and form, no melody and no lyrics. Simplifications, per the one-chord-per-bar rule: (1) the 12-bar strain uses the standard quick-change chart -- C7 in bar 2 (some editions hold G), C7 in bar 10, and a D7 turnaround in bar 12 as played at jams (the printed final cadence rests on G); where the sheet moves twice inside a bar the bar's primary chord is written. (2) The 16-bar tango strain's i-V7 oscillation is regularised into two-bar Gm/D7 cells; editions vary in exact cadence placement, but the harmonic content (tonic minor against D7 under the habanera figure) is not in doubt. (3) The intro and outro are chord-only vamps in the manner of the published introduction -- arrangement, not tune. Encoded in 4/4 as universally played; if reading an edition that notates the habanera strain in 2/4, two written bars map to one bar here at half the written tempo.

notes: Multi-strain form: a 12-bar blues strain in G major (verse and chorus share these changes) and a 16-bar habanera strain in G minor. The tango section is the drama of the piece -- the drop to the tonic minor with the habanera pulse -- and the return to the major blues afterwards lands like a release; jam the energy arc accordingly. Both strains repeat cleanly, so any form entry can be looped for solos.
